[LLM] Vulnerable HTTP/2 server inventory (CVE-2026-49975 — nginx/mod_http2/Envoy/IIS) Weaponization High
Surfaces hosts running HTTP/2-capable web servers at versions the Calif researchers proved vulnerable to the HTTP/2 Bomb (nginx pre-1.29.8, Apache httpd with mod_http2 < 2.0.41, Envoy 1.37.2, and IIS on Windows Server 2025 where no patch yet exists). Inventory-based hunt that prioritises patching/HTTP-2-disable work and identifies the attack surface for the follow-up runtime detections. Rationale: Pivots on CveId == CVE-2026-49975 (the assigned identifier from the Apache disclosure) plus the exact vulnerable build strings the article names (nginx 1.29.7, mod_http2 < 2.0.41, Envoy 1.37.2, IIS on Windows Server 2025). Joining DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing focuses triage on hosts the article notes are most exposed — CDN-fronted estates are 'more difficult to target'. Cross-checked against Tenable's CVE record and the upstream nginx commit adding max_headers. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.calif.io/p/codex-discovered-a-hidden-http2-bomb • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2026-49975 • https://github.com/nginx/nginx/commit/365694160a85229a7cb006738de9260d49ff5fa2 • https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q2/790

[LLM] HTTP/2 Bomb stall signature — long-hung HTTP/2 requests with near-zero response bytes Command & Control Medium
Detects the zero-window flow-control hold half of the HTTP/2 Bomb: the server has allocated memory but never emits a response because the client advertises a zero-byte WINDOW. On the wire this shows up as small numbers of inbound HTTP/2 requests from a single source IP that each persist for tens of seconds while the server returns almost no bytes. Targets IIS / nginx / Apache / Envoy access logs and inbound network telemetry. Rationale: Encodes the exact wire signature the article describes: 'requests are never fully completed, and the allocated memory keeps growing' via zero-byte WINDOW + tiny WINDOW_UPDATE responses. TimeTaken ≥ 20s with scBytes ≤ 1024 captures Apache/Envoy 32-GB-in-20s and IIS 64-GB-in-45s profiles. Few-but-long (HungReqs ≥ 3) — not a flood — matches Calif's 'single-client' claim. Cross-checked against the Calif technical write-up (blog.calif.io) and SecurityWeek's reproduction summary. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.calif.io/p/codex-discovered-a-hidden-http2-bomb • https://www.securityweek.com/http-2-bomb-exploit-knocks-web-servers-offline-in-seconds/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-http2-bomb-vulnerability-allows.html
ATT&CKT1499.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
// HTTP/2 Bomb stall signature — multiple held inbound HTTP/2 connections from a single source
let WebProcs = dynamic(["nginx.exe","httpd.exe","w3wp.exe","envoy.exe","iisexpress.exe","apache2","nginx","httpd"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where ActionType =~ "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort in (443, 8443, 80)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any (WebProcs)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"        // ignore intra-DC health checks
| summarize ConnCount       = count(),
            DistinctRemotePorts = dcount(RemotePort),
            FirstConn        = min(Timestamp),
            LastConn         = max(Timestamp),
            HoldSeconds      = datetime_diff('second', max(Timestamp), min(Timestamp))
        by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where ConnCount >= 20 and HoldSeconds >= 20    // 20+ simultaneous inbound h2 conns held ≥20s — matches Apache/Envoy 32GB-in-20s profile
| project FirstConn, LastConn, DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, ConnCount, DistinctRemotePorts, HoldSeconds
| order by ConnCount desc
// HTTP/2 Bomb stall — IIS/web access logs showing held requests with near-zero response
let IISHung =
    W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
    | where TimeTaken >= 20000           // ≥20s — article: 32GB consumed in ~20s on Apache/Envoy
    | where scBytes  <= 1024             // server emitted no real response body
    | where csMethod !in~ ("PUT","POST") or csBytes < 65536   // exclude legitimate slow large uploads
    | summarize HungReqs = count(),
                DistinctUris = dcount(csUriStem),
                TotalHoldMs = sum(TimeTaken),
                MaxHoldMs   = max(TimeTaken),
                SampleAgent = any(csUserAgent),
                FirstSeen   = min(TimeGenerated),
                LastSeen    = max(TimeGenerated)
            by cIP, sSiteName, Computer
    | where HungReqs >= 3                // bomb is FEW long streams, not a flood
    | project FirstSeen, LastSeen, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, HungReqs, DistinctUris, MaxHoldMs, TotalHoldMs, SampleAgent;
let AsimHung =
    ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
    | where NetworkDuration >= 20000
    | where HttpResponseBodyBytes <= 1024
    | summarize HungReqs = count(),
                TotalHoldMs = sum(NetworkDuration),
                MaxHoldMs   = max(NetworkDuration),
                DistinctUris = dcount(Url),
                FirstSeen   = min(TimeGenerated),
                LastSeen    = max(TimeGenerated)
            by SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname
    | where HungReqs >= 3
    | project FirstSeen, LastSeen, Computer=DvcHostname, sSiteName="", cIP=SrcIpAddr, HungReqs, DistinctUris, MaxHoldMs, TotalHoldMs, SampleAgent="";
union IISHung, AsimHung
| order by MaxHoldMs desc
(source:iis OR source:nginx.access OR source:apache.access) @http.method:* (@duration:>=20000 OR @time_taken:>=20000) (@http.response_content_length:<1024 OR @sc_bytes:<1024 OR @network.bytes_written:<1024) -@http.url_details.path:(/healthz OR /ping OR /events OR /stream OR /sse OR /ws OR /websocket)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ConnectionDirection=1
| ContextImageFileName=/(nginx|httpd|w3wp|envoy|apache2)(\.exe)?$/i
| RemotePort=/^(443|8443|80)$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, ContextImageFileName], function=count(), limit=1000)
| count >= 20
# log group: /aws/applicationelb/access-logs   (or wherever your ALB access logs flow into CWLI)
fields @timestamp, client_ip, target_processing_time, request_processing_time, response_processing_time, sent_bytes, received_bytes, request_url, elb_status_code, protocol
| filter protocol = "HTTP/2"
      and target_processing_time >= 20
      and sent_bytes <= 1024
      and request_url not like /(\/healthz|\/ping|\/sse|\/events|\/stream|\/ws)/i
| stats count(*) as hung_reqs, max(target_processing_time) as max_hold, sum(sent_bytes) as total_sent by client_ip, request_url
| filter hung_reqs >= 3
| sort max_hold desc

[LLM] Web-tier worker crash / OOM storm following HTTP/2 Bomb memory exhaustion Actions on Objectives High
Detects the impact phase: rapid worker-process recycles or OOM-killer events on hosts running nginx, Apache httpd, IIS (w3wp.exe), or Envoy. The HTTP/2 Bomb causes 32–64 GB of RAM to be consumed in 10–45 seconds; on Linux this triggers oom-killer; on Windows IIS this triggers Application Pool crash-recycles and Application Error 1000 events naming w3wp.exe. Designed to fire even if the on-wire UC2 missed the request shape. Rationale: Built directly on the article's impact description — 32–64 GB RAM exhaustion in 10–45 seconds. On Linux this surfaces as oom-killer entries naming nginx/httpd/envoy in Syslog; on Windows IIS the bomb crash-loops the application pool, producing Application Error 1000 events naming w3wp.exe plus rapid 4688 NewProcessName=w3wp.exe spawns. Pivots on web-server binary names from the article's tested versions. Cross-checked against the Calif technical write-up and the oss-sec disclosure. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.calif.io/p/codex-discovered-a-hidden-http2-bomb • https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q2/790 • https://gbhackers.com/http-2-bomb-remote-dos-exploit/
ATT&CKT1499.003 T1499.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
// HTTP/2 Bomb impact — web worker restart storm (process pool churn from OOM)
let WebProcs = dynamic(["nginx.exe","httpd.exe","apache2","httpd","w3wp.exe","envoy.exe","nginx"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where FileName in~ WebProcs or FileName has_any (WebProcs)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize SpawnCount    = count(),
            DistinctPids  = dcount(ProcessId),
            FirstSpawn    = min(Timestamp),
            LastSpawn     = max(Timestamp),
            SampleParent  = any(InitiatingProcessFileName),
            SampleCmd     = any(ProcessCommandLine)
        by DeviceName, FileName, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where SpawnCount >= 10                           // 10 worker (re)starts in 5 min — well above normal recycle rate
| extend StormWindowSec = datetime_diff('second', LastSpawn, FirstSpawn)
| project FirstSpawn, LastSpawn, StormWindowSec, DeviceName, FileName, SpawnCount, DistinctPids, SampleParent, SampleCmd
| order by SpawnCount desc
// HTTP/2 Bomb impact — OOM-killer (Linux) and Application Error 1000 (Windows IIS) targeting web workers
let LookbackHours = 1h;
let LinuxOOM =
    Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
    | where SyslogMessage has "oom-killer" or (SyslogMessage has "Out of memory" and SyslogMessage has "Killed process")
    | where SyslogMessage has_any ("nginx","httpd","apache2","envoy")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName="oom-killer", Detail=SyslogMessage, Platform="Linux";
let WinIISCrash =
    Event
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
    | where EventID == 1000 and Source has "Application Error"
    | where RenderedDescription has_any ("w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","envoy.exe")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName="Application Error 1000", Detail=RenderedDescription, Platform="Windows";
let WinWorkerStorm =
    SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where NewProcessName has_any ("\\w3wp.exe","\\nginx.exe","\\httpd.exe","\\envoy.exe")
    | summarize Spawns=count(), arg_min(TimeGenerated, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName) by Computer, NewProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
    | where Spawns >= 10
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName=NewProcessName, Detail=strcat("WorkerStorm spawns=", tostring(Spawns)), Platform="Windows";
union LinuxOOM, WinIISCrash, WinWorkerStorm
| summarize CrashEvents=count(), arg_min(TimeGenerated, ProcessName, Detail), arg_max(TimeGenerated, ProcessName) by Computer, Platform
| where CrashEvents >= 3
| order by CrashEvents desc
(source:linux.syslog @log.message:*oom-killer* @log.message:(*nginx* OR *httpd* OR *apache2* OR *envoy*)) OR (source:windows.security @EventID:1000 (@Image:(*\\w3wp.exe OR *\\W3WP.exe OR *\\nginx.exe OR *\\Nginx.exe OR *\\httpd.exe OR *\\Httpd.exe OR *\\envoy.exe OR *\\Envoy.exe))) OR (source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @NewProcessName:(*\\w3wp.exe OR *\\W3WP.exe OR *\\nginx.exe OR *\\Nginx.exe OR *\\httpd.exe OR *\\envoy.exe))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(nginx|httpd|w3wp|envoy|apache2)(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName], function=[count(as=spawns), min(_time, as=first_spawn), max(_time, as=last_spawn)])
| spawns >= 10
| storm_window_sec := last_spawn - first_spawn

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-49975")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-49975")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

A new malware campaign is turning trusted cloud infrastructure against the organizations that rely on it. Known as HazyBeacon and tracked under cluster identifier CL-STA-1020, the campaign targets government networks across Southeast Asia. Rather than using easily blocked servers, the threat actors hide inside one of the world&#8217;s most trusted platforms, Amazon Web Services (AWS). | order by TimeGenerated desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["4931df8650521cfd686782919bda0f376475f9fc5f1fee9d7cf3a4e0d9c73e30", "d20b536c88ecd326f79d7a9180f41a2e47a40fcf2cc6a2b02d68a081c89eaeaa", "304c615f4a8c2c2b36478b693db767d41be998032252c8159cc22c18a65ab498", "f0c9481513156b0cdd216d6dfb53772839438a2215d9c5b895445f418b64b886", "3255798db8936b5b3ae9fed6292413ce20da48131b27394c844ecec186a1e92f", "279e60e77207444c7ec7421e811048267971b0db42f4b4d3e975c7d0af7f511e", "d961aca6c2899cc1495c0e64a29b85aa226f40cf9d42dadc291c4f601d6e27c3"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2024-55591", "CVE-2025-32433", "CVE-2025-33073", "CVE-2024-3400", "CVE-2023-4966", "CVE-2020-5135")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2024-55591", "CVE-2025-32433", "CVE-2025-33073", "CVE-2024-3400", "CVE-2023-4966", "CVE-2020-5135")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2024-55591", "CVE-2025-32433", "CVE-2025-33073", "CVE-2024-3400", "CVE-2023-4966", "CVE-2020-5135")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2024-55591", "CVE-2025-32433", "CVE-2025-33073", "CVE-2024-3400", "CVE-2023-4966", "CVE-2020-5135")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:

      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["025fc0976c548fb5a880c83ea3eb21a5f23c5d53c4e51e862bb893c11adf712a", "1334f0189a8e6dbc48456fa4b482c5726ab7609f7fa652fcc4c1a96f2334436f", "1af419b36a5edefef387409e2b3248c9223f7dc49a4f7b15ea095d371c3a70b2", "22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "24ac3588fb8cfbff63b7fdfcbc7dec1f3c60e54e6f949dd69d68e89e0c89d966", "2ed9494e9b7b68415b4eb151c922c82c0191294d0aa443dd2cb5133e6bfe3d5d", "3ab9575225e00a83a4ac2b534da5a710bdcf6eb72884944c437b5fbe5c5c9235", "3c2182cb0bc7528829ef03f1b1745a92bcc47d917eb8870862488f21fdf1a6d6", "1eece1e1ba4b96e6c784729f0608ad2939cfb67bc4236dfababbe1d09268960c", "5dc607c8990841139768884b1b43e1403496d5a458788a1937be139594f01dca", "788ba200f776a188c248d6c2029f00b5d34be45d4444f7cb89ffe838c39b8b19"]);
union

        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] CVE-2022-0492 cgroup release_agent container escape — unshare + rdma mount + release_agent chain Exploitation High
Hunts the published exploit signature for CVE-2022-0492: a process inside a container invokes 'unshare' to create user/cgroup namespaces and then mounts the RDMA cgroup controller, with a command line referencing the cgroup 'release_agent' file. This is the exact behavioural chain documented by Aqua Security, Palo Alto Unit 42 and Sysdig for the CISA-KEV-listed Linux kernel container escape. Rationale: Anchored on the published Falco/Sysdig rule for CVE-2022-0492 (unshare + mount + rdma + release_agent) and the Aqua / Unit 42 exploit walkthrough that the article explicitly cites. Cross-checked Unit 42 (https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2022-0492-cgroups/), Aqua Security blog, and Sysdig (https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-mitigating-cve-2022-0492-sysdig). The 'release_agent' string + 'rdma' cgroup controller combo is article-specific and not matched by generic LOLBin / privilege-escalation rules. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2022-0492-cgroups/ • https://www.aquasec.com/blog/new-linux-kernel-vulnerability-escaping-containers-by-abusing-cgroups/ • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-mitigating-cve-2022-0492-sysdig • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2022-0492 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611/
ATT&CKT1611 T1068 T1059.004

   or (ProcessCommandLine has "mount" and ProcessCommandLine has "rdma" and ProcessCommandLine has "cgroup")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "unshare" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)-[UrmC]+|--user|--mount|--cgroup")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "release_agent"
   or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "mount" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "rdma" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "cgroup")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: CVE-2022-0492 cgroup release_agent Container Escape via unshare
id: 7b3e8c1d-6a4f-4e21-9b8d-1f2a5c3d9e10
description: Detects the published CVE-2022-0492 exploit chain where a process uses unshare to create user/cgroup namespaces and mounts the rdma cgroup controller with a command line referencing the cgroup release_agent file. Pattern from Aqua Security, Unit 42 and Sysdig writeups.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2022-0492-cgroups/
  - https://www.aquasec.com/blog/new-linux-kernel-vulnerability-escaping-containers-by-abusing-cgroups/
  - https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-mitigating-cve-2022-0492-sysdig
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-warns-of-active-attacks-exploiting-android-linux-bugs/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/03
tags:
  - attack.t1611
  - attack.t1068
  - attack.privilege_escalation
  - cve.2022.0492
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_unshare:
    Image|endswith: '/unshare'
  selection_chain:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'release_agent'
  selection_mount:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'mount'
      - 'rdma'
      - 'cgroup'
  condition: selection_unshare and (selection_chain or selection_mount)
falsepositives:
  - Container security research / pentesting
  - Kubernetes upgrade tooling that legitimately remounts cgroupfs
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.name:unshare OR @process.command_line:*unshare*) (@process.command_line:*release_agent* OR (@process.command_line:*rdma* AND @process.command_line:*cgroup*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ImageFileName=/\/unshare$/i OR CommandLine=/unshare/i)
| (CommandLine=/release_agent/i OR (CommandLine=/rdma/i AND CommandLine=/cgroup/i))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="unshare" OR Processes.process="*unshare*") AND (Processes.process="*release_agent*" OR (Processes.process="*mount*" AND Processes.process="*rdma*" AND Processes.process="*cgroup*")) by Processes.dest Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
[LLM] CVE-2022-0492 — Write to cgroup release_agent file inside /sys/fs/cgroup hierarchy Installation High
Detects creation or modification of a 'release_agent' file inside the cgroup filesystem — the terminal step of the CVE-2022-0492 container-escape chain where the attacker plants a command (executed as root on the host) into release_agent and triggers notify_on_release. Article cross-referenced Aqua Security + Unit 42 research on this exact primitive. Rationale: release_agent is a cgroups v1-specific primitive — there is almost no benign reason for non-runtime code to write to it. Anchored on the article's named function (cgroup_release_agent_write) plus the Unit 42 / Aqua exploit chain (https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2022-0492-cgroups/). Detects the terminal step of the exploit even if the attacker writes from a shell rather than unshare directly (covering UC1's blind spots). Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2022-0492-cgroups/ • https://www.aquasec.com/blog/new-linux-kernel-vulnerability-escaping-containers-by-abusing-cgroups/ • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-mitigating-cve-2022-0492-sysdig • https://book.hacktricks.wiki/en/linux-hardening/privilege-escalation/docker-security/docker-breakout-privilege-escalation/docker-release_agent-cgroups-escape.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611/
ATT&CKT1611 T1574 T1547
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName == "release_agent"
| where FolderPath has "/sys/fs/cgroup/" or FolderPath has "/cgroup/"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("systemd", "kubelet", "containerd", "containerd-shim", "runc", "crun", "dockerd")
             and InitiatingProcessAccountName == "root")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName == "release_agent"
| where TargetFilePath has "/sys/fs/cgroup/" or TargetFilePath has "/cgroup/"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileWritten")
| where not (ActingProcessName has_any ("systemd", "kubelet", "containerd", "runc", "crun", "dockerd")
             and ActorUsername == "root")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: CVE-2022-0492 cgroup release_agent File Write
id: 9f4a2c7e-3d8b-4c5a-a6f1-2e8d9b3c4f50
description: Detects creation or modification of a release_agent file inside the /sys/fs/cgroup hierarchy. This is the persistence/trigger primitive of the CVE-2022-0492 container escape — the file is invoked by the kernel as root on the host when notify_on_release fires.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2022-0492-cgroups/
  - https://www.aquasec.com/blog/new-linux-kernel-vulnerability-escaping-containers-by-abusing-cgroups/
  - https://terenceli.github.io/%E6%8A%80%E6%9C%AF/2022/03/06/cve-2022-0492
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-warns-of-active-attacks-exploiting-android-linux-bugs/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/03
tags:
  - attack.t1611
  - attack.t1574
  - attack.privilege_escalation
  - cve.2022.0492
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '/release_agent'
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '/sys/fs/cgroup/'
      - '/cgroup/'
  filter_runtime:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/systemd'
      - '/kubelet'
      - '/containerd'
      - '/containerd-shim'
      - '/runc'
      - '/crun'
      - '/dockerd'
  condition: selection and not filter_runtime
falsepositives:
  - Container runtime startup (filtered above)
  - Manual sysadmin tuning of legacy cgroup v1 notify_on_release behaviour
level: high
source:linux.auditd (@file.path:*\/sys\/fs\/cgroup\/*\/release_agent OR @file.path:*\/cgroup\/*\/release_agent) (@auditd.type:PATH OR @evt.name:open OR @evt.name:openat OR @evt.name:write) -@process.name:(systemd OR kubelet OR containerd OR containerd-shim OR runc OR crun OR dockerd)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| regex("\\/release_agent$", field=TargetFileName)
| regex("\\/(sys\\/fs\\/)?cgroup\\/", field=TargetFileName)
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/\/(systemd|kubelet|containerd|containerd-shim|runc|crun|dockerd)$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.process_name) as process values(Filesystem.user) as user values(Filesystem.action) as action from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="release_agent" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/release_agent") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*/sys/fs/cgroup/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/cgroup/*") AND Filesystem.action IN ("create","modify","write","created","modified") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-48595", "CVE-2022-0492")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-48595", "CVE-2022-0492")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

What 345 Days of Untested Exposure Looks Like at a Bank

BleepingComputer
2026-06-03 4 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

A two-week penetration test can leave roughly 345 days of real-world exposure unvalidated. Sprocket Security explores why continuous testing is becoming critical as attack surfaces constantly change. [...]

ATT&CKT1190 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Acer Wave 7 unauthenticated acer_cgi.log credential disclosure (CVE-2026-49200) Exploitation High
Hunts HTTP requests to the /acer_cgi.log endpoint on Acer Wave 7 mesh routers (admin URLs http://192.168.76.1 / http://acerconnect.com). This file is reachable without auth and contains cleartext web + Telnet credentials, so any GET to that exact path is the entire CVE-2026-49200 exploit primitive. Rationale: The article explicitly names acer_cgi.log as the unauthenticated file containing cleartext web + Telnet credentials (CVE-2026-49200). Pivoting on that exact URI substring catches every PoC and exploit attempt with effectively zero benign traffic since the file is not a normal user-facing resource. Cross-referenced with the admin endpoints 192.168.76.1 and acerconnect.com given in the article body to scope to actual Acer Wave 7 targets. No external corroboration searched — same-day vendor advisory referenced in article body.
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "acer_cgi.log"
   or (RemoteUrl has_any ("acerconnect.com", "192.168.76.1") and AdditionalFields has "acer_cgi.log")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountDomain
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(RequestURL)
| where RequestURL has "acer_cgi.log"
| extend AdminTarget = iff(DestinationIP == "192.168.76.1" or DestinationHostName has "acerconnect.com", "acer-admin", "other")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName,
          RequestURL, RequestMethod, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, ReceivedBytes, SentBytes,
          RequestClientApplication, AdminTarget
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Acer Wave 7 upload.cgi backup tamper for persistent backdoor (CVE-2026-49201) Installation Medium
Hunts POST requests to /upload.cgi on Acer Wave 7 routers carrying re-encrypted system backups. CVE-2026-49201 leaks a hardcoded AES key in upload.cgi that lets an attacker decrypt, modify (inject backdoor) and re-encrypt a backup so the device persists the implant on restore. Suspicious-shape POSTs to that endpoint from non-admin sources are the only on-wire artefact of the exploit. Rationale: Article identifies upload.cgi as the backup-processing binary holding the hardcoded AES key (CVE-2026-49201). POST is the only HTTP method consistent with the documented backup upload/restore action; pairing path + method + admin-destination (192.168.76.1 / acerconnect.com) tightens to the actual exploit primitive. Bytes-in floor (>1024) screens out probing or empty form submissions. Falcon and CloudWatch left empty — Falcon FDR doesn't carry HTTP URL paths, and the telemetry is web/network not AWS-native.
ATT&CKT1601.002 T1554 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has "upload.cgi"
   or (RemoteUrl has_any ("acerconnect.com", "192.168.76.1") and AdditionalFields has "upload.cgi")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountDomain,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where isnotempty(RequestURL)
| where RequestURL has "upload.cgi"
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| extend BackupBytes = toint(ReceivedBytes)
| extend AdminTarget = iff(DestinationIP == "192.168.76.1" or DestinationHostName has "acerconnect.com", "acer-admin", "other")
| where AdminTarget == "acer-admin" or BackupBytes > 1024
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName,
          RequestURL, RequestMethod, BackupBytes, SentBytes, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct,
          RequestClientApplication, AdminTarget
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Argamal COM Hijack of Windows Color System Calibration Loader CLSID Installation High
Detects HKCU CLSID hijack of the Windows Color System Calibration Loader {B210D694-C8DF-490D-9576-9E20CDBC20BD} or the Stage1 staging CLSID {722D0F89-B69C-4700-AE8C-4A44350E4876} where InprocServer32 / ShellFolder points to a DLL in AppData\Local. This is Argamal's login-trigger persistence anchor. Rationale: Anchored on the two exact CLSIDs from the article ({B210D694-...} Calibration Loader and {722D0F89-...} Stage1 staging) plus the HKCU AppData\Local InprocServer32 payload location — the combination is article-specific and not produced by any legitimate Color System software (which writes HKLM).

[LLM] Argamal MI_V / MI_V2 Environment Variable Stage Handoff Installation High
Detects creation of the HKCU\Environment\MI_V or MI_V2 value used by Argamal Stage1 PowerShell to hand off the Base64-encoded Stage2 payload to a delayed scheduled task. The variable name is unique to this family. Rationale: MI_V / MI_V2 is a unique-to-Argamal env-var name documented in the Securelist write-up as the Stage1→Stage2 handoff. Anchored on the exact HKCU\Environment subkey + literal value names — no legitimate software writes these names.
ATT&CKT1140 T1546.015 T1027.013
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey endswith "\\Environment"

[LLM] Argamal Stage2 BITSAdmin Pull of zaesdl.dat from GitHub Command & Control High
Detects bitsadmin.exe invoked with /transfer (or /addfile + /resume) downloading the AES-encrypted RAT payload named zaesdl.dat — Argamal's Stage2 retrieval pattern using GitHub-hosted infrastructure. Rationale: Anchored on the exact payload filename (zaesdl.dat) and Argamal's documented use of GitHub-hosted Stage2 retrieved via bitsadmin. The combination of bitsadmin + github + .dat extension is extremely uncommon outside this family.

| where NewProcessName endswith "\\bitsadmin.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("/transfer","/addfile","/create","/resume")
| where CommandLine has_any ("zaesdl.dat","raw.githubusercontent.com","github.com","gist.githubusercontent.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

[LLM] Argamal RAT C2 Beacon — 186.158.223.35 / freeddns / kozow / ignorelist / UDP-57441 / TCP-3747 Command & Control High
Detects connections to the Argamal RAT C2 infrastructure: hardcoded IP 186.158.223.35, the three dyndns FQDNs (asper1.freeddns.org, winst0.kozow.com, country1.ignorelist.com), and the malware's unusual UDP/57441 heartbeat / TCP/3747 extended-mode / UDP/63559 payload-update ports. Rationale: Hardcoded IP 186.158.223.35 plus three named dyndns FQDNs and the three unusual ports (UDP/57441 heartbeat, TCP/3747 extended-mode, UDP/63559 payload-update) are pulled verbatim from the Securelist IOC section. The port-only branch is gated by AppData\Local origin to suppress unrelated egress.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1095 T1568.002 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RemoteIP == "186.158.223.35")
    or (RemoteUrl in~ ("asper1.freeddns.org","winst0.kozow.com","country1.ignorelist.com"))
    or (RemotePort in (57441,3747,63559) and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "AppData\\Local")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (DstIpAddr == "186.158.223.35")
    or (DstHostname in~ ("asper1.freeddns.org","winst0.kozow.com","country1.ignorelist.com"))
    or (DstPortNumber in (57441,3747,63559))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, NetworkBytes

[LLM] Argamal Scheduled Task Pointing at AppData\Local DLL via Color System Calibration Loader Installation Medium
Detects scheduled task creation/modification where the Argamal Stage1 PowerShell registers a delayed (3-day) trigger or repurposes the \Microsoft\Windows\WindowsColorSystem\Calibration Loader task to launch a random-named DLL from %USER%\AppData\Local. Catches the persistence and the delayed-detonation primitives in one shot. Rationale: References the exact task path \Microsoft\Windows\WindowsColorSystem\Calibration Loader, the MI_V env-var fed to Stage2, and the AppData\Local DLL target — all article-specific. Catches both the 3-day-delayed task primitive and the recurring login-trigger task in one rule.
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1546.015 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("schtasks.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/create","/change","Register-ScheduledTask","New-ScheduledTask")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Calibration Loader","WindowsColorSystem","MI_V")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "AppData\\Local" and ProcessCommandLine has ".dll" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("rundll32","regsvr32","-Command","-EncodedCommand"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\schtasks.exe" or NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("/create","/change","Register-ScheduledTask","New-ScheduledTask")
| where CommandLine has_any ("Calibration Loader","WindowsColorSystem","MI_V")
   or (CommandLine has "AppData\\Local" and CommandLine has ".dll")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

[LLM] Argamal Loader Artifacts — natives2_blob.bin / Modified ffmpeg.dll IOC Sweep Installation High
Detects the Argamal loader files on disk: the natives2_blob.bin script-executor DLL by filename, the known modified ffmpeg.dll by SHA1 (42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85), and the script-executor DLL by SHA1 (edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d). Triggers on file write, file open, or image load. Rationale: Hash IOC sweep + named-artifact hunt. The filename natives2_blob.bin is unique to Argamal (does not appear in any legitimate ffmpeg / game shipment) and the two SHA1s are confirmed-malicious per the Kaspersky write-up. Union across DeviceFileEvents and DeviceImageLoadEvents catches both the drop and the load.
ATT&CKT1574.001 T1204.002 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
union
  (DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(90d) | where FileName =~ "natives2_blob.bin" or SHA1 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85","edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="FileEvent", ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA1, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
  (DeviceImageLoadEvents | where Timestamp > ago(90d) | where FileName =~ "ffmpeg.dll" and SHA1 == "42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="ImageLoad", ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA1, FileOriginUrl="", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
  (DeviceImageLoadEvents | where Timestamp > ago(90d) | where SHA1 == "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="ImageLoad", ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA1, FileOriginUrl="", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "natives2_blob.bin"
    or TargetFileSHA1 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85","edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA1, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85", "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d") or SHA1 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85", "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d") or MD5 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85", "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85", "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d") or SHA1 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85", "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d") or MD5 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85", "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85", "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New HTTP/2 Bomb Vulnerability Allows Remote DoS on NGINX, Apache, IIS, Envoy & Cloudflare

The Hacker News
2026-06-03 9 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have discovered a remote denial-of-service exploit that affects major web servers, including NGINX, Apache HTTPD, Microsoft IIS, Envoy, and Cloudflare Pingora. The vulnerability has been codenamed HTTP/2 Bomb by Calif. "The vulnerable behavior exists in each server's default HTTP/2 configuration," the company said, adding it was discovered by OpenAI Codex by chaining

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Vulnerable web server inventory for HTTP/2 Bomb (CVE-2026-49975, nginx <1.29.8, mod_http2 <2.0.41, IIS/Envoy/Pingora unpatched)
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Web server worker process recycle/crash burst (nginx, httpd, w3wp, envoy) — HTTP/2 Bomb memory-exhaustion symptom · [LLM] IIS Application Pool fatal recycle / WAS worker termination — HTTP/2 Bomb on Windows IIS · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
[LLM] Vulnerable web server inventory for HTTP/2 Bomb (CVE-2026-49975, nginx <1.29.8, mod_http2 <2.0.41, IIS/Envoy/Pingora unpatched) Weaponization High
Surfaces hosts running web servers vulnerable to the HTTP/2 Bomb: Apache httpd (CVE-2026-49975), nginx prior to 1.29.8, plus any IIS / Envoy / Cloudflare Pingora install since those products had no patch at disclosure. Triage list for emergency mitigation (max_headers / `Protocols http/1.1` / `http2 off`). Rationale: Article names exact fixed versions (nginx 1.29.8+, mod_http2 v2.0.41) and explicitly states IIS/Envoy/Pingora have no patch at disclosure — those are non-CVE-trackable exposures, so inventory sweep is required alongside the CVE match. Cross-checked CVE-2026-49975 against securityweek.com and the openwall oss-security thread (https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/06/03/3) — both confirm same-day fix by Stefan Eissing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.securityweek.com/http-2-bomb-exploit-knocks-web-servers-offline-in-seconds/ • https://blog.calif.io/p/codex-discovered-a-hidden-http2-bomb • https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/06/03/3 • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2026-49975

    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)

         or SoftwareName has "envoy"

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP

[LLM] Web server worker process recycle/crash burst (nginx, httpd, w3wp, envoy) — HTTP/2 Bomb memory-exhaustion symptom Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for abnormally rapid re-spawning of web server worker processes on a single host, the on-host symptom of HTTP/2 Bomb memory exhaustion: a single client can pin 32GB on Apache/Envoy in ~20s, after which the worker is killed and recycled. A run of >5 worker spawns in 10 minutes on a single host is well above normal recycle cadence. Rationale: The article quantifies the attack — '32GB of server memory in about 20 seconds' on Apache/Envoy from a single client. The deterministic on-host symptom is the worker process being killed (OOM / app-pool recycle) and re-spawned in a tight loop. Threshold of >5 per 10m chosen because normal IIS app-pool recycle cadence is 0–1 per host per hour; nginx/httpd worker churn is similarly low under steady state. Cross-checked attack mechanics against the Calif blog (https://blog.calif.io/p/codex-discovered-a-hidden-http2-bomb). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.calif.io/p/codex-discovered-a-hidden-http2-bomb • https://www.securityweek.com/http-2-bomb-exploit-knocks-web-servers-offline-in-seconds/
ATT&CKT1499.003 T1499.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
// HTTP/2 Bomb on-host symptom: worker recycle burst on a single device
let WebWorkers = dynamic(["nginx.exe","httpd.exe","apache.exe","w3wp.exe","envoy.exe","pingora.exe","nginx","httpd","apache2","envoy","pingora"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where FileName in~ (WebWorkers) or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (WebWorkers)
| extend Worker = iff(FileName in~ (WebWorkers), FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize SpawnCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SampleParent = any(InitiatingProcessFileName),
            SampleCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine)
            by DeviceName, Worker, bin_at(Timestamp, 10m, ago(24h))
| where SpawnCount > 5
| extend BurstWindow = strcat(format_datetime(Timestamp,'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm'),' - ',format_datetime(Timestamp + 10m,'HH:mm'))
| project FirstSeen, LastSeen, DeviceName, Worker, SpawnCount, BurstWindow, SampleParent, SampleCmd
| order by SpawnCount desc
let WebWorkers = dynamic(["nginx.exe","httpd.exe","apache.exe","w3wp.exe","envoy.exe","pingora.exe"]);

| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where EventID == 4688
| extend ImgName = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| where ImgName in (WebWorkers)
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"

            SampleParent = any(ParentProcessName),
            SampleCmd = any(CommandLine)
            by Computer, ImgName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)

| order by SpawnCount desc

[LLM] IIS Application Pool fatal recycle / WAS worker termination — HTTP/2 Bomb on Windows IIS Actions on Objectives Medium
Targets the Windows-IIS-specific symptom of HTTP/2 Bomb. Because IIS had no patch at article disclosure, exploitation is the most likely path. Microsoft-Windows-WAS logs EID 5009 (worker process terminated unexpectedly), 5011 (fatal communication error), 5074 (worker exceeded health-monitoring threshold), and 5117 (rapid-fail protection tripped) — clusters of these in a short window on internet-facing IIS hosts are a strong DoS signal. Rationale: Article explicitly states 'Microsoft IIS, Envoy, and Cloudflare Pingora - No patch available as of writing' — IIS exposure cannot be remediated by upgrade alone at disclosure, so post-compromise detection matters most for IIS. WAS event IDs (5009/5011/5074/5117) are the canonical Windows-side log of worker-process death, which is exactly what HPACK-bookkeeping memory exhaustion produces (32GB pinned ⇒ worker killed). Cross-checked via Cybersecuritynews and gbhackers coverage of the same CVE. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/http-2-bomb-remote-dos-exploit/ • https://gbhackers.com/http-2-bomb-remote-dos-exploit/amp/ • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2026-49975
ATT&CKT1499.004
Data sourcesApplication_State
// IIS App Pool fatal-recycle burst — System log via Microsoft-Windows-WAS
let WasFatal = dynamic([5009, 5011, 5074, 5117]);
WindowsEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Provider == "Microsoft-Windows-WAS"
| where EventID in (WasFatal)
| extend AppPool = extract(@"application pool '([^']+)'", 1, tostring(EventData))
| summarize CrashCount = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            EventIDs = make_set(EventID, 10),
            AppPools = make_set(AppPool, 10)
            by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 15m)
| where CrashCount > 3
| project FirstSeen, LastSeen, Computer, CrashCount, EventIDs, AppPools
| order by CrashCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
