source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE ((@process.name:rm @process.command_line:*\-rf* (@process.command_line:*\ \~\/* OR @process.command_line:*\ \$HOME* OR @process.command_line:*\~\/Documents*) (@process.parent.name:(node OR bun OR sh OR bash OR npm))) OR @process.command_line:*IfYouInvalidateThisTokenItWillNukeTheComputerOfTheOwner*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (regex("IfYouInvalidateThisTokenItWillNukeTheComputerOfTheOwner", field=CommandLine))
   OR (ImageFileName=/\/rm$/i AND regex("\\-rf", field=CommandLine) AND regex("(\\s~\\/?|\\s\\$HOME|~\\/Documents)", field=CommandLine) AND ParentBaseFileName=/^(node|bun|sh|bash|npm)$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName, ParentCommandLine], function=count())

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m

| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966", "8bf051251ec3b973e39a313547e53421a2f8d2f6", "608d01124cd6b5b8c55888e984b4c4d9b06fa686", "ab9903d9edc720d1e11ea7d3d3e7a1c456f44ff7") or SHA1 in~ ("7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966", "8bf051251ec3b973e39a313547e53421a2f8d2f6", "608d01124cd6b5b8c55888e984b4c4d9b06fa686", "ab9903d9edc720d1e11ea7d3d3e7a1c456f44ff7") or MD5 in~ ("7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966", "8bf051251ec3b973e39a313547e53421a2f8d2f6", "608d01124cd6b5b8c55888e984b4c4d9b06fa686", "ab9903d9edc720d1e11ea7d3d3e7a1c456f44ff7")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966", "8bf051251ec3b973e39a313547e53421a2f8d2f6", "608d01124cd6b5b8c55888e984b4c4d9b06fa686", "ab9903d9edc720d1e11ea7d3d3e7a1c456f44ff7") or SHA1 in~ ("7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966", "8bf051251ec3b973e39a313547e53421a2f8d2f6", "608d01124cd6b5b8c55888e984b4c4d9b06fa686", "ab9903d9edc720d1e11ea7d3d3e7a1c456f44ff7") or MD5 in~ ("7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966", "8bf051251ec3b973e39a313547e53421a2f8d2f6", "608d01124cd6b5b8c55888e984b4c4d9b06fa686", "ab9903d9edc720d1e11ea7d3d3e7a1c456f44ff7")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966", "8bf051251ec3b973e39a313547e53421a2f8d2f6", "608d01124cd6b5b8c55888e984b4c4d9b06fa686", "ab9903d9edc720d1e11ea7d3d3e7a1c456f44ff7"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45247")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has

// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45247")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] DNS / web resolution of WeedHack distribution and C2 domains · [LLM] JAR file written to disk with WeedHack distribution URL provenance
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Java executing Minecraft-client-named JAR from Downloads or Temp · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Java process beaconing to WeedHack C2 infrastructure · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Java process reading browser, Discord, Steam or Telegram credential stores · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
[LLM] Java process beaconing to WeedHack C2 infrastructure Command & Control High
Detects java.exe/javaw.exe initiating outbound network sessions to the WeedHack receiver/remote-control domains or the staging IP 45.141.119.34. Because the C2 hosts are dedicated to the MaaS dashboard, any hit from a Java parent is high-fidelity infostealer beacon or premium-tier RAT traffic. Rationale: Both the IP 45.141.119.34 and the receiver.*/whreceive.*/telemetrydata.to host set are named in the article and corroborated by McAfee Labs and CyberInsider write-ups. Scoping by java.exe/javaw.exe parent yields near-zero baseline FP because legitimate Java apps don't dial .cy/.ru receivers. Cross-checked against: • https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/weedhack-minecraft-malware-as-a-service-campaign-research/ • https://cyberinsider.com/weedhack-minecraft-malware-campaign-infects-over-116000-pcs/ • https://0xresetti.github.io/weedhack.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1219 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where RemoteIP == "45.141.119.34"
    or RemoteUrl has_any ("receiver.cy","whreceive.ru","whreceiver.ru","remotev2.whreceive.ru","telemetrydata.to")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr == "45.141.119.34"
    or DstHostname has_any ("receiver.cy","whreceive.ru","whreceiver.ru","remotev2.whreceive.ru","telemetrydata.to")
| where SrcUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WeedHack C2 Beacon from Java Process
id: 6f3b8c2a-7e94-4d52-a3f1-9c1d4e8b27a1
description: Detects java.exe/javaw.exe initiating network connections to known WeedHack receiver / remote-control C2 infrastructure (BleepingComputer / McAfee, June 2026).
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-116-000-minecraft-systems-infected-in-weedhack-malware-campaign/
  - https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/weedhack-minecraft-malware-as-a-service-campaign-research/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/03

  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1219
  - attack.t1568

  category: network_connection

[LLM] DNS / web resolution of WeedHack distribution and C2 domains Delivery High
Org-wide signal on any DNS query or web request to the WeedHack distribution sites (weedhack.cy, weedhack.to, marsalek.cy, huehnchenfarm.ru) or receiver C2 hosts. Catches the lure-site visit phase before the JAR is ever executed and works even on hosts without EDR. Rationale: Both the distribution domains (weedhack.cy, weedhack.to, marsalek.cy, huehnchenfarm.ru) and the receiver/C2 set are explicitly listed in the article's pre-extracted IOCs and re-confirmed in the McAfee Labs blog and 0xresetti's WeedHack technical analysis. Domain-IOC alerting carries near-zero FP because the names are unique and unrelated to legitimate Minecraft infrastructure. Cross-checked against: • https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/weedhack-minecraft-malware-as-a-service-campaign-research/ • https://0xresetti.github.io/weedhack.html • https://cyberinsider.com/weedhack-minecraft-malware-campaign-infects-over-116000-pcs/

    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Source = "DeviceNetworkEvents"),
  (DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)

    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort = int(null), Source = "DnsQueryResponse")
| order by Timestamp desc

[LLM] Java executing Minecraft-client-named JAR from Downloads or Temp Installation Medium
Hunts java.exe/javaw.exe spawned with a JAR file path whose name matches the lure-client list called out by McAfee (Meteor, Wurst, Aristois, LiquidBounce, Impact, Skytils, Radium, Future, Inertia, Cornos, WWE, 3arthh4ck, Salhack, Phobos, Gamesense) and that lives under user Downloads, Temp, or .minecraft\mods. Catches the WeedHack detonation moment. Rationale: The 14-name lure list is verbatim from the article's SEO-poisoning paragraph plus Skytils called out in the screenshot, and the download paths are from the kill-chain Phase 2 detection hint. Pairing client-name + downloads-path-prefix is the article-specific combination — a power user might run java with a JAR, but the specific named lures from this campaign in Downloads/Temp is high-signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/weedhack-minecraft-malware-as-a-service-campaign-research/ • https://0xresetti.github.io/weedhack.html
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.006

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".jar"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\.minecraft\mods\")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (MinecraftLures)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let MinecraftLures = dynamic(["Meteor","Wurst","Aristois","LiquidBounce","Impact","Skytils","Radium","Future","Inertia","Cornos","WWE","3arthh4ck","Salhack","Phobos","Gamesense"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith @"\java.exe" or ActingProcessName endswith @"\javaw.exe"

| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\.minecraft\mods\")

[LLM] Java process reading browser, Discord, Steam or Telegram credential stores Actions on Objectives High
Hunts for java.exe/javaw.exe touching the specific credential-storage files WeedHack targets: Chromium Login Data / Cookies / Local State across 36 browsers, Discord leveldb, Steam ssfn / config.vdf, Telegram tdata, and wallet-extension Local Extension Settings. No legitimate Java process needs to read these paths. Rationale: The credential-store path set comes directly from kill-chain Phase 4: '36 browsers, 56 cryptocurrency add-ons, 12 desktop cryptocurrency wallet apps, Discord, Steam, and Telegram credentials'. McAfee's report and 0xresetti's reverse-engineering confirm the stealer enumerates Chromium User Data\*\Login Data, Discord leveldb, Steam ssfn, and Telegram tdata. Threshold of 2+ distinct paths avoids single-file-read FPs from legit Java apps. Cross-checked against: • https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/weedhack-minecraft-malware-as-a-service-campaign-research/ • https://0xresetti.github.io/weedhack.html
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
let CredPaths = dynamic([@"\Login Data", @"\Cookies", @"\Local State", @"\discord\Local Storage\leveldb", @"\discordcanary\Local Storage\leveldb", @"\discordptb\Local Storage\leveldb", @"\Steam\config\config.vdf", @"\Steam\ssfn", @"\Steam\config\loginusers.vdf", @"\Telegram Desktop\tdata", @"\Local Extension Settings\"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any (CredPaths)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize HitCount = count(), DistinctPaths = dcount(FolderPath), SamplePaths = make_set(FolderPath, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
          by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| where DistinctPaths >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
let CredPaths = dynamic([@"\Login Data", @"\Cookies", @"\Local State", @"\discord\Local Storage\leveldb", @"\Steam\config\config.vdf", @"\Steam\ssfn", @"\Telegram Desktop\tdata", @"\Local Extension Settings\"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith @"\java.exe" or ActingProcessName endswith @"\javaw.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (CredPaths)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| summarize HitCount = count(), DistinctPaths = dcount(TargetFilePath), SamplePaths = make_set(TargetFilePath, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine
| where DistinctPaths >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\java.exe OR *\javaw.exe OR *\Java.exe OR *\JAVA.EXE OR *\JavaW.exe OR *\JAVAW.EXE) @TargetFilename:(*\\Login\ Data* OR *\\Cookies* OR *\\Local\ State* OR *\\discord\\Local\ Storage\\leveldb* OR *\\Steam\\ssfn* OR *\\Steam\\config\\config.vdf OR *\\Telegram\ Desktop\\tdata* OR *\\Local\ Extension\ Settings*)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/\\java(w)?\.exe$/i

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, UserName], function={ DistinctPaths := count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true) | HitCount := count() })
| DistinctPaths > 1

[LLM] JAR file written to disk with WeedHack distribution URL provenance Delivery High
Catches the delivery moment — a .jar dropped by a browser (chrome.exe/msedge.exe/firefox.exe/brave.exe) where FileOriginUrl or FileOriginReferrerUrl points to a WeedHack distribution domain. Targets the SEO-poisoning and YouTube-comment-link arrival path before java is even invoked. Rationale: Combines file extension (.jar), browser parent, and FileOriginUrl-derived provenance — three article-specific anchors. The WeedHack distribution domains are unique to this campaign per McAfee Labs and 0xresetti's analysis, so any browser-downloaded JAR with this provenance is effectively a confirmed delivery. Cross-checked against: • https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/weedhack-minecraft-malware-as-a-service-campaign-research/ • https://0xresetti.github.io/weedhack.html • https://cyberinsider.com/weedhack-minecraft-malware-campaign-infects-over-116000-pcs/

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

    selection_file:

            - '\Cookies'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Telegram Bot API C2 channel used by AI-built ransomware toolkit (non-IM/non-browser egress) · [LLM] First-time egress to *.workers.dev (Cloudflare Worker C2 redirector) from non-browser process · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
[LLM] Telegram Bot API C2 channel used by AI-built ransomware toolkit (non-IM/non-browser egress) Command & Control High
Hunts for processes other than known browsers and Telegram desktop clients reaching api.telegram.org — the toolkit Sophos analysed routes beacon traffic through the Telegram Bot API instead of direct C2. Custom Rust/Go loaders and curl/PowerShell wrappers are the typical callers in this campaign. Rationale: Targets the article's explicit 'Telegram bot API-based external C2 mechanism that routed communication through Telegram's infrastructure rather than using direct connections.' Tightens the existing generic Sigma (detection.fyi) by also flagging unsigned/non-IM-vendor process metadata characteristic of Rust/Go beacons the toolkit produces. Cross-checked Sophos's own blog post and Splunk Security Content's 'Windows DNS Query Request by Telegram Bot API' rule for non-duplication. Cross-checked against: • https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2026/06/02/ai-built-ransomware-toolkit/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/02/ai-agents-edr-evasion-techniques/ • https://detection.fyi/sigmahq/sigma/network/dns/net_dns_susp_telegram_api/ • https://research.splunk.com/network/86f66f44-94d9-412d-a71d-5d8ed0fef72e/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Resolution
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.telegram.org" or RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)api\.telegram\.org/bot[A-Za-z0-9:_\-]+"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("telegram.exe","telegramdesktop.exe","updater.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe","slack.exe","discord.exe","teams.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where isempty(InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName)
   or InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !in~ ("Microsoft Corporation","Google LLC","Mozilla Corporation","Telegram Messenger LLP","Slack Technologies, Inc.","Discord Inc.")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName,
          InitiatingProcessVersionInfoProductName,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
let TelegramHosts = dynamic(["api.telegram.org"]);
let KnownIM = dynamic(["telegram.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","slack.exe","discord.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe","teams.exe"]);
let CmdlineHits = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where CommandLine has "api.telegram.org"
    | extend ProcName = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
    | where ProcName !in (KnownIM)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account=SubjectUserName, ProcessName=NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Src="ProcessCmdLine";
let DnsHits = DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Name =~ "api.telegram.org"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, Src="DNS";
union CmdlineHits, DnsHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-Browser Network Connection to Telegram Bot API (AI-built Ransomware Toolkit C2)
id: 7d9c8e2f-3b41-4a16-9e8c-2f1d7b4a9c01
status: experimental
description: Detects DNS resolution of api.telegram.org from processes other than known browsers/Telegram desktop, indicative of the AI-built ransomware toolkit's Telegram Bot API C2 (Sophos, 2026-06-02).
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/ai-built-ransomware-toolkit-automates-edr-evasion-ad-discovery/
  - https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2026/06/02/ai-built-ransomware-toolkit/
author: SOC Detection Eng
date: 2026/06/02
tags:
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1102
  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: dns
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName|endswith: 'api.telegram.org'
  filter_browsers:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\firefox.exe'
      - '\brave.exe'

      - '\teams.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_browsers

  - Internal chatops/monitoring bots using Telegram for alerting
  - Approved red-team engagements
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:22 @QueryName:api.telegram.org -@Image:(*\\telegram.exe OR *\\Telegram.exe OR *\\TELEGRAM.EXE OR *\\chrome.exe OR *\\Chrome.exe OR *\\msedge.exe OR *\\firefox.exe OR *\\Firefox.exe OR *\\brave.exe OR *\\slack.exe OR *\\Slack.exe OR *\\discord.exe OR *\\Discord.exe OR *\\teams.exe OR *\\Teams.exe OR *\\opera.exe OR *\\iexplore.exe)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/^api\.telegram\.org$/i
| ContextImageFileName!=/\\(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|opera|iexplore|telegram|telegramdesktop|updater|slack|discord|teams)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count(as=Hits))
| Hits > 0

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmd values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*api.telegram.org*" OR Processes.process="*api.telegram.org/bot*") by Processes.dest Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT match(process_name, "(?i)^(chrome|msedge|firefox|telegram|brave|slack|discord|opera|iexplore|teams)\.exe$") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmd values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*api.telegram.org*" OR Processes.process="*api.telegram.org/bot*") by Processes.dest Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT match(process_name, "(?i)^(chrome|msedge|firefox|telegram|brave|slack|discord|opera|iexplore|teams)\.exe$") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
[LLM] First-time egress to *.workers.dev (Cloudflare Worker C2 redirector) from non-browser process Command & Control Medium
Detects a host reaching a Cloudflare Worker URL that has not been observed in the prior 30-day baseline, when the caller is not a sanctioned browser. The Sophos toolkit specifically uses a Cloudflare Worker as a front-end redirector to obscure the actual backend C2 server. Rationale: Targets the article's call-out that the toolkit deploys 'A Cloudflare Worker acting as a front-end redirector to obscure the actual backend C2 server.' Anti-pattern guidance in the house style says don't blanket-allow workers.dev — instead flag the first-time-per-host. Pairs with UC1 (Telegram) — same host hitting both is a confirmed-bad signal. Cross-checked against hunt.io's 'Russian-Speaking Threat Actor Abuses Cloudflare & Telegram' write-up showing the same TTP combination. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/russian-actor-cloudflare-phishing-telegram-c2 • https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2026/06/02/ai-built-ransomware-toolkit/

| where RemoteUrl endswith ".workers.dev"
| join kind=leftanti Known on RemoteUrl
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe","slack.exe","teams.exe","outlook.exe","webex.exe","safari.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let Lookback = 30d;
let Recent = 1h;
let Known = DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(Lookback) .. ago(Recent))
    | where Name endswith ".workers.dev"

DnsEvents

| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), QueryCount=count(), HostCount=dcount(Computer), ClientIPs=make_set(ClientIP, 25) by Name

[LLM] Payload staging in user 'Documents\test' folder — AI-built ransomware toolkit drop path Installation High
Detects executable, DLL, or script files being written to '\Users\<user>\Documents\test\' — the exact staging directory Sophos observed in the victim environment for this toolkit's Cobalt Strike profiles, Python loaders, and shellcode-injection scripts. Catches operator-driven file drops before payload execution. Rationale: Pivots on the exact victim-side staging path Sophos disclosed: 'payloads stored in C:\Users\User\Documents\test'. Generalised to any user profile (any '\Users\<x>\Documents\test\') to catch the operator's standard drop pattern across hosts in the same environment. Extension filter targets the languages/file types Sophos enumerated (Python, Rust, Go, Cobalt Strike DLLs). Cross-checked against: • https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2026/06/02/ai-built-ransomware-toolkit/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/02/ai-agents-edr-evasion-techniques/
ATT&CKT1105 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)\\Users\\[^\\]+\\Documents\\test\\"
| where FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".dll" or FileName endswith ".ps1"
   or FileName endswith ".py"  or FileName endswith ".bat" or FileName endswith ".cmd"
   or FileName endswith ".js"  or FileName endswith ".vbs" or FileName endswith ".hta"
   or FileName endswith ".rs"  or FileName endswith ".go"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileSize
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)\\Users\\[^\\]+\\Documents\\test\\"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("exe","dll","ps1","py","bat","cmd","js","vbs","hta","rs","go")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, TargetFileSize
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Payload Staging in User Documents\test Folder (AI-built Ransomware Toolkit)
id: 8b4f5d10-9c72-4d1a-83fa-7a6c1f0b5d12
status: experimental
description: Detects executable/DLL/script files being written to a 'Documents\test\' subdirectory under any user profile — the exact staging path Sophos observed for the AI-built ransomware toolkit's payloads (Cobalt Strike profiles, Python injectors, Rust/Go beacons).
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/ai-built-ransomware-toolkit-automates-edr-evasion-ad-discovery/
  - https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2026/06/02/ai-built-ransomware-toolkit/

date: 2026/06/02

detection:

  - QA engineer compiling test artefacts to this location
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\Documents\\test\\* OR *\\Documents\\Test\\* OR *\\Documents\\TEST\\*) @TargetFilename:(*.exe OR *.dll OR *.ps1 OR *.py OR *.bat OR *.cmd OR *.js OR *.vbs OR *.hta)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\Users\\[^\\]+\\Documents\\test\\/i
| TargetFileName=/\.(exe|dll|ps1|py|bat|cmd|js|vbs|hta|rs|go)$/i

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"

| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-48595")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-48595")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Gamaredon Exploits WinRAR to Deliver GammaWorm and GammaSteel Against Ukraine

The Hacker News
2026-06-02 19 use cases 8 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

The Russian hacking group known as Gamaredon has been attributed to the continued exploitation of a WinRAR vulnerability to deliver multiple malware families aimed at data theft and propagation. Per Sekoia, the activity involves the weaponization of CVE-2025-8088, a path traversal flaw in WinRAR, to launch an HTML Application payload dubbed GammaPhish, which is then used to retrieve an

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 path traversal — file written from WinRAR into Startup folder · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] GammaPhish HTA auto-execution — mshta.exe launching from user Startup folder · [LLM] GammaWorm NTFS Alternate Data Stream module hide — script-host writes file with ADS suffix · [LLM] GammaSteel registry-staged module fan-out — PowerShell writes many binary blobs under one key · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] GammaWorm Telegram/Telegraph/Teletype/Cloudflare-Workers DDR resolution via curl from script host · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] GammaWorm USB / network-share propagation — script process mass-creates LNK files on removable or remote drives · [LLM] GammaSteel S3 exfiltration — script/PowerShell HTTP egress to AWS S3 bucket · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
[LLM] WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 path traversal — file written from WinRAR into Startup folder Delivery High
Hunts the GammaPhish initial-access signature: a WinRAR / UnRAR / RAR process writes a file into a Windows Startup directory. CVE-2025-8088 lets a malicious archive traverse out of the chosen extraction path; Gamaredon weaponises it to drop an HTA dropper that auto-runs at next logon. Rationale: Article + Sekoia explicitly state the WinRAR exploit drops an HTA into the Startup directory via path traversal. Pairing the archive-tool image with the Startup destination is the cleanest single-event signature for CVE-2025-8088 exploitation. Cross-checked Sekoia blog and follow-on Hacker News CVE-2025-8088 coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/01/google-warns-of-active-exploitation-of.html • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/gamaredon-worm-ntfs-data-streams/
ATT&CKT1203 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winrar.exe","unrar.exe","rar.exe") | where FolderPath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\" | where FileName !endswith ".log" and FileName !endswith ".tmp" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, ArchiveTool=InitiatingProcessFileName, ArchiveCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, DroppedFile=FileName, DropPath=FolderPath, SHA256 | order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where ActingProcessName has_any ("winrar.exe","unrar.exe","rar.exe") | where TargetFilePath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\" | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256 | order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 Path Traversal Write Into Startup Folder
id: f1c5b3a2-9e7d-4b6a-b1f0-3d8c9e2a4711
description: WinRAR / UnRAR / RAR process writes a file directly into a Windows Startup directory — indicative of CVE-2025-8088 path-traversal exploitation used by Gamaredon to drop GammaPhish HTA.
references:
    - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/gamaredon-exploits-winrar-to-deliver.html
    - https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/02
tags:
    - attack.t1203
    - attack.t1547.001
    - attack.initial_access
    - attack.persistence
    - cve.2025.8088
logsource:
    category: file_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_proc:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\winrar.exe'
            - '\unrar.exe'
            - '\rar.exe'
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains: '\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\'
    condition: selection_proc and selection_path
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrator manually packaging Startup-folder shortcuts via WinRAR
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@Image:(*\\WinRAR.exe OR *\\winrar.exe OR *\\UnRAR.exe OR *\\unrar.exe OR *\\Rar.exe OR *\\rar.exe)) (@TargetFilename:(*\\Start\ Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\* OR *\\start\ menu\\programs\\startup\\*))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/\\(winrar|unrar|rar)\.exe$/i TargetFileName=/\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_name) as file_name values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_name IN ("winrar.exe","unrar.exe","rar.exe","WinRAR.exe") OR Filesystem.process_path="*\\WinRAR\\*") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Microsoft\\Windows\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_name) as file_name values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.process_name IN ("winrar.exe","unrar.exe","rar.exe","WinRAR.exe") OR Filesystem.process_path="*\\WinRAR\\*") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Microsoft\\Windows\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
[LLM] GammaPhish HTA auto-execution — mshta.exe launching from user Startup folder Installation High
Hunts the GammaPhish auto-run: at next logon, explorer.exe launches mshta.exe against an HTA that CVE-2025-8088 dropped into the Startup folder. Pairing the parent (explorer) with the binary (mshta) and the HTA's path (Startup) is a high-fidelity catch for the post-exploit handoff to GammaLoad. Rationale: Sekoia and Hacker News articles describe the GammaPhish HTA being dropped directly into the Startup folder by the WinRAR exploit, which then auto-launches via mshta at logon. Combining explorer→mshta parentage with the Startup path eliminates the bulk of mshta noise from legitimate HTAs hosted elsewhere. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/ • https://cyberpress.org/gamaredon-apt-hides-malware/
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where FileName =~ "mshta.exe" | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe" | where ProcessCommandLine has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\" or ProcessCommandLine has_any (".hta",".HTA") and ProcessCommandLine has "Startup" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ChildImage=FolderPath, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256 | order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where EventID == 4688 | where NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe" | where ParentProcessName endswith "\\explorer.exe" | where CommandLine has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\" | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine | order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] GammaWorm Telegram/Telegraph/Teletype/Cloudflare-Workers DDR resolution via curl from script host Command & Control High
Hunts the GammaWorm dead-drop-resolver step: a VBScript host (wscript / cscript / mshta) spawns curl.exe to fetch a hardcoded public Telegram channel page (t.me/telegra.ph) or its Teletype.in / Cloudflare Workers fall-back, from which the actual C2 address is parsed. Catches the exact platform abuse Sekoia documents. Rationale: Sekoia's report explicitly names Telegram, Telegra.ph, Teletype.in, and Cloudflare Workers as Gamaredon's DDR platforms, and curl as the GammaWorm fetch tool. Pairing curl with a script-host parent and one of these four domains is single-event-shape and very rare in a legit corporate environment. One of the article IOCs (bold.zsjtn41091.workers.dev) is a Cloudflare Workers DDR endpoint. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/ • https://cyberpress.org/gamaredon-apt-hides-malware/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where FileName =~ "curl.exe" | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe") | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("t.me/","telegra.ph","teletype.in",".workers.dev") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ScriptHost=InitiatingProcessFileName, ScriptCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, CurlCmd=ProcessCommandLine | order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where ActingProcessName endswith "curl.exe" | where ParentProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe") | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("t.me/","telegra.ph","teletype.in",".workers.dev") | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine | order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] GammaWorm USB / network-share propagation — script process mass-creates LNK files on removable or remote drives Actions on Objectives High
Hunts GammaWorm's lateral-movement pattern: a VBScript host (wscript / cscript) writes many .lnk files to a removable drive or network share within a short window, while concurrently setting the hidden attribute on existing directories. The shortcut-replacing technique is Gamaredon's documented spread vector for USB and SMB. Rationale: Article specifies GammaWorm 'hide legitimate directories in network shares and USB drives and replace with malicious Windows Shortcut (LNK) files.' Detection keys on script-host parentage + drive letter outside C: or UNC root + LNK extension + burst count — none of these alone are unusual, but the combination is. Skipped Sigma because the threshold/grouping is multi-event correlation. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/ • https://cyberpress.org/gamaredon-apt-hides-malware/

[LLM] GammaWorm NTFS Alternate Data Stream module hide — script-host writes file with ADS suffix Installation Medium
Hunts the GammaWorm defence-evasion technique: a VBScript host writes one of its core modules into an Alternate Data Stream (filename:streamname pattern) on a host file. Sekoia documents this as the primary on-disk hiding mechanism for the worm's modules. Rationale: Article + Infosecurity Magazine + Sekoia all confirm GammaWorm uses NTFS Alternate Data Streams to conceal its core modules. Script-host parentage + ADS-shape filename + Zone.Identifier exclusion is the cleanest single-event match. Cross-checked Infosecurity Magazine for technique confirmation. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/gamaredon-worm-ntfs-data-streams/ • https://undercodenews.com/silent-infiltration-russian-linked-gamaredon-worm-exploits-windows-hidden-streams-to-haunt-ukrainian-systems-without-a-trace-video/
ATT&CKT1564.004

DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") | where FileName matches regex @"^[^:]+:[^:\\/]+$" | where FileName !endswith ":Zone.Identifier" and FileName !endswith ":SmartScreen" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, ScriptHost=InitiatingProcessFileName, ScriptCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ADSFile=FileName, ADSPath=FolderPath | order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") | where TargetFileName matches regex @"^[^:]+:[^:\\/]+$" | where TargetFileName !endswith ":Zone.Identifier" | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath | order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] GammaSteel registry-staged module fan-out — PowerShell writes many binary blobs under one key Installation Medium
Hunts GammaSteel's documented self-staging behaviour: the PowerShell-based stealer writes ~71 DPAPI-encrypted modules as binary values into a single registry key, used as its in-memory loading store. The fan-out of binary registry values from a single PowerShell process to one parent key is article-specific and very rare. Rationale: Sekoia and follow-on coverage describe GammaSteel staging 71 encrypted PowerShell modules in the registry, protected by Windows DPAPI. Threshold ≥20 distinct binary values under one HKCU/HKLM\Software key written by a single PowerShell/wscript process in 30 minutes catches the staging without over-firing on legitimate per-value config writes. Multi-event correlation, so Sigma is intentionally skipped. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/ • https://cyberpress.org/gamaredon-apt-hides-malware/
ATT&CKT1112 T1140 T1055.012
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
DeviceRegistryEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryValueModified") | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe") | where RegistryValueType in ("Binary","None") | where RegistryKey startswith @"HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\" or RegistryKey startswith @"HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\" | summarize DistinctValues=dcount(RegistryValueName), TotalWrites=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Sample=any(RegistryValueData) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RegistryKey, bin(Timestamp, 30m) | where DistinctValues >= 20 | order by DistinctValues desc
ImRegistryEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | where EventType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryValueModified") | where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe") | where RegistryValueType in ("Binary","REG_BINARY") | summarize DistinctValues=dcount(RegistryValue), TotalWrites=count() by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, RegistryKey, bin(TimeGenerated, 30m) | where DistinctValues >= 20
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:13 (@Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\WScript.exe)) (@TargetObject:(*\\Software\\* OR *\\SOFTWARE\\*))
#event_simpleName=AsepValueUpdate ContextImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i | regex("\\\\Software\\\\", field=RegObjectName, flags=i) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RegObjectName], function={distinct_values := count(field=RegValueName, distinct=true) | total := count()}) | distinct_values >= 20
ENDPOINT

[LLM] GammaSteel S3 exfiltration — script/PowerShell HTTP egress to AWS S3 bucket Actions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the GammaSteel exfiltration path: a script host or PowerShell process not normally seen on the wire issues an outbound HTTPS connection to *.s3.amazonaws.com (or s3.<region>.amazonaws.com) to upload harvested files. Article specifies S3 as the primary exfil with attacker-controlled web servers as a fallback. Rationale: Article explicitly names AWS S3 as GammaSteel's exfil destination with attacker-controlled fallback. The hunt isolates the unusual combination of script-host parentage and S3 egress — neither AWSPowerShell nor aws-cli are in the included process list, so legitimate S3 backup activity from a developer workstation falls outside scope. Tier set to hunting because S3 is widely used; analyst should pivot from any hit to the parent process chain. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/fsbs-matryoshka-1-3-gamaredons-gifts-that-keeps-unpacking-gammaphish-and-gammaworm/ • https://cyberpress.org/gamaredon-apt-hides-malware/

ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK

| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
